name: CN III Oculomotor nerve
modality: General somatic efferent and preganglionic parasympathetic (general visceral efferent).
course: Motor and parasympathetic fascicles arise in the rostral midbrain, pass ventrally and emerge in the interpeduncular fossa. The cisternal nerve passes between PCA and SCA, traverses the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. Superior and inferior divisions supply extraocular/eyelid muscles and the ciliary ganglion.
function: Supplies medial, superior and inferior rectus, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris. Superior/inferior recti are tested for elevation/depression with the eye abducted; inferior oblique elevates the adducted eye. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers synapse in the ciliary ganglion; short ciliary nerves then supply sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. Pupil involvement varies by lesion.

afferent: Axons arise from oculomotor somatic motor neurons and Edinger-Westphal preganglionic neurons; supranuclear inputs terminate centrally rather than traveling in the nerve.
efferent: Superior division: superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris
Inferior division: medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to ciliary ganglion

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Ptosis, diplopia and impaired adduction/elevation/depression may occur, with a down-and-out eye in a complete somatic palsy. Pupil constriction and accommodation may also be impaired. Pupil sparing does not exclude a compressive lesion such as an aneurysm.

An ipsilateral third-nerve palsy with contralateral weakness or ataxia suggests accompanying midbrain motor or crossed cerebellar-output involvement. Weber, Claude and Benedikt labels describe overlapping patterns rather than mandatory full syndromes.
Combined III/IV/VI and trigeminal deficits can arise from cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure lesions. Pupil involvement is variable and cannot distinguish the site by itself.

Acute third-nerve dysfunction can accompany posterior communicating aneurysm or transtentorial herniation. The clinical sequence is variable; a fixed pupil-first, palsy-second, weakness-third progression is not reliable.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, ocular nerves, actions and pupillary pathways, printed pp. 568-580 (PDF pp. 594-606).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, gaze and ocular motor palsies, printed pp. 585-592 (PDF pp. 611-618).
Patel and Burdon, Isolated third cranial nerve palsies: modern management principles, Eye (2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8727561/ (pupil sparing does not exclude compression).
contextNote: This nerve is displayed as an authored course tube, not a segmented specimen. The central nuclear crossing pattern differs from the ipsilateral targets of the peripheral nerve: superior-rectus nuclear fibers cross, and levator control is bilateral. Coordinates, tube thickness and orbital waypoints are conceptual.

name: CN IV Trochlear nerve
course: Axons from the inferior-collicular-level trochlear nucleus pass dorsally and cross in the superior (anterior) medullary velum, then emerge below the inferior colliculus. The nerve courses around the midbrain, passes through the cavernous sinus lateral wall and superior orbital fissure, and supplies the superior oblique on the same side as the exiting peripheral nerve.
function: Supplies superior oblique, which intorts the eye and depresses it most effectively when adducted, with an abducting component. The nucleus supplies the contralateral superior oblique because its fibers cross before dorsal emergence.

afferent: Trochlear motor nucleus; central ocular motor inputs reach the nucleus, not the peripheral nerve.
efferent: Superior oblique of the ipsilateral orbit relative to the post-crossing nerve

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Vertical/torsional diplopia and hypertropia may be more evident looking down with the eye adducted. Head tilt toward the affected side can worsen hypertropia and patients may compensate by tilting away. This pattern is helpful but not uniquely diagnostic; skew deviation and other ocular conditions can mimic it.

A lesion of the nucleus or fibers before their decussation affects the contralateral superior oblique. A lesion after crossing affects the ipsilateral eye; a midline decussation lesion can affect both. Trauma, congenital disorders, microvascular disease and other causes can produce trochlear palsy.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, ocular nerves, actions and pupillary pathways, printed pp. 568-580 (PDF pp. 594-606).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, gaze and ocular motor palsies, printed pp. 585-592 (PDF pp. 611-618).
Patel and Burdon, Isolated third cranial nerve palsies: modern management principles, Eye (2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8727561/ (pupil sparing does not exclude compression).
contextNote: Authored schematic course. Pre-crossing nuclear/fascicular injury and post-crossing nerve injury have different laterality; a single tube cannot certify the intramedullary crossing geometry.

name: CN V Trigeminal nerve
modality: General somatic afferent and branchial motor (special visceral efferent).
course: Large sensory and smaller motor roots emerge at the lateral mid-pons. Most primary sensory neurons are in the trigeminal ganglion; jaw-proprioceptive neurons are in the mesencephalic nucleus. V1 enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure, V2 passes through foramen rotundum and V3 through foramen ovale. The motor root joins V3.
function: Carries general sensation from much of the face, cornea, oral/nasal cavities, teeth and cranial dura. V3 motor fibers supply mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini. CN V supplies the afferent limb of the corneal blink reflex; CN VII supplies its motor limb.

afferent: Peripheral sensory axons associated with trigeminal ganglion neurons
Jaw proprioceptive primary afferents associated with the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus
efferent: Central sensory processes to principal and spinal trigeminal nuclei; proprioceptive connections to mesencephalic/motor circuits
Motor axons from trigeminal motor nucleus through V3 to first-pharyngeal-arch muscles

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Lesions can impair sensation in one or more divisions and reduce the V1 afferent corneal reflex. Pterygoid weakness can cause the jaw to deviate toward the weak side on opening. Division patterns narrow localization but do not uniquely identify one foramen.

Brief recurrent shock-like facial pain may be triggered by innocuous stimuli. Neurovascular compression is one recognized mechanism; secondary causes include demyelination or mass lesions. Sensory deficits prompt investigation but no age or examination rule proves a particular cause.

Spinal trigeminal injury can cause ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss together with contralateral body pain-temperature loss when adjacent ascending body pathways are involved. Concentric facial loss is possible but not obligatory.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, trigeminal pathways and branches, printed pp. 508-512 (PDF pp. 534-538).
contextNote: The drawn common-root/V3 course does not depict all V1/V2/V3 branches. No root crossing occurs; many second-order trigeminothalamic fibers cross within the brainstem. This is not a second crossing of primary nerve fibers.
geometryNote: Spatial course withheld: the former root-to-ganglion route headed posteriorly toward an unvalidated target. Corrected CN V root, divisions, foramina and clinical descriptions remain available as text.

name: CN VI Abducens nerve
course: Motor fascicles from the caudal pontine abducens nucleus emerge at the pontomedullary sulcus near the midline. The nerve ascends along the clivus through Dorello canal, traverses the cavernous sinus near the internal carotid and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
function: Supplies ipsilateral lateral rectus for eye abduction. Abducens internuclear neurons cross and ascend in the opposite MLF to the oculomotor nucleus; those axons are central gaze connections and are not carried in CN VI.

afferent: Abducens somatic motor neurons; gaze-control input reaches the nucleus centrally.

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Impaired abduction produces horizontal diplopia, often greater toward the weak side. Nuclear injury instead usually impairs conjugate gaze toward that side because motor and internuclear neurons are affected.

clinical.syndrome: Raised intracranial pressure or local injury
clinical.findings: The long intracranial course can be affected by raised pressure as a false-localizing sign, skull-base disease, cavernous sinus lesions, trauma or microvascular disease. Laterality and recovery are variable.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, ocular nerves, actions and pupillary pathways, printed pp. 568-580 (PDF pp. 594-606).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 13, gaze and ocular motor palsies, printed pp. 585-592 (PDF pp. 611-618).
Patel and Burdon, Isolated third cranial nerve palsies: modern management principles, Eye (2022), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8727561/ (pupil sparing does not exclude compression).
contextNote: Authored schematic course; the nerve and the nuclear internuclear pathway are distinct. Clival/skull-base/orbital relationships have no registered skull model.

name: CN VII Facial nerve
modality: Branchial motor, preganglionic parasympathetic, taste (special visceral afferent), and a small general sensory component.
course: Facial motor fibers loop around the abducens nucleus, then emerge with the nervus intermedius at the pontomedullary/cerebellopontine angle. The nerve enters the internal acoustic meatus and facial canal. Greater petrosal and chorda tympani branches carry parasympathetic/taste fibers; motor fibers exit the stylomastoid foramen and branch within the parotid gland.
function: Supplies facial-expression muscles, stapedius, posterior digastric and stylohyoid; conveys anterior-two-thirds tongue taste; provides parasympathetic supply to lacrimal/nasal/palatal glands through pterygopalatine ganglion and submandibular/sublingual glands through submandibular ganglion. Passing through the parotid does not give it parotid secretomotor function.

afferent: Taste and small general sensory afferents with cell bodies in geniculate ganglion; central taste input reaches rostral solitary nucleus and general sensory input spinal trigeminal complex.
efferent: Branchial motor axons from facial nucleus to second-pharyngeal-arch muscles
Superior salivatory/lacrimal preganglionic axons to pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Nuclear, fascicular or peripheral motor injury can weaken the entire ipsilateral face, including forehead and eye closure. More proximal lesions may add hyperacusis, taste or secretomotor changes; these are not universal.

Unilateral supranuclear lesions often predominantly affect the contralateral lower face because upper facial input is more bilateral. Forehead sparing is a useful relative pattern, not an absolute rule. A pontine lesion can produce a peripheral-pattern palsy with other brainstem signs.
Bell palsy, infection, inflammatory disease, tumor and traumatic injury are among possible peripheral causes. A facial-weakness pattern alone does not establish Bell palsy.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, facial nerve and taste, printed pp. 513-518 (PDF pp. 539-544).
contextNote: Authored schematic common course; branch-level facial canal and gland pathways are text only. Lesion position determines whether taste, tear/salivary or stapedius deficits accompany facial weakness.

name: CN VIII Vestibulocochlear nerve
modality: Special somatic afferent; small peripheral auditory/vestibular efferent components also exist.
course: Cochlear and vestibular divisions connect the inner ear through the internal acoustic meatus to the lateral pontomedullary/cerebellopontine-angle region. Primary cochlear neurons reside in spiral ganglion and vestibular neurons in vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion.
function: Cochlear fibers transmit sound information to cochlear nuclei. Vestibular fibers carry head-motion/position signals to vestibular nuclei and directly to cerebellar circuitry, supporting balance and vestibulo-ocular reflexes. The downstream ocular motor or spinal output of those reflexes is carried by other pathways.

afferent: Spiral ganglion neurons receiving cochlear hair-cell input
Vestibular ganglion neurons receiving semicircular-canal and otolith input
efferent: Central primary afferents to cochlear nuclei, vestibular nuclei and cerebellar targets
Small olivocochlear and vestibular efferent systems return from the brainstem toward inner-ear targets

bloodSupply: The inner ear and intrameatal nerve are supplied by the labyrinthine artery, usually arising from AICA but sometimes from the basilar artery. The central cochlear/vestibular nuclear region has separate overlapping vertebrobasilar branches.

clinical.findings: Peripheral cochlear/nerve injury can cause ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus or imbalance; vestibular injury can cause vertigo and nystagmus. Central and peripheral patterns overlap and the symptoms do not establish one site on their own.
Vestibular schwannoma and other masses may affect hearing/balance and, with extension, adjacent nerves or brainstem. Hearing loss need not be the first or only finding.

AICA/labyrinthine ischemia can mimic peripheral vestibular illness, sometimes with hearing loss. Acute vestibular examination requires the appropriate clinical setting and expertise; an atlas pattern is insufficient to exclude stroke.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, auditory and vestibular pathways, printed pp. 518-529 (PDF pp. 544-555).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, vertebrobasilar anatomy and lateral pontine syndrome, printed pp. 651-656 (PDF pp. 677-682).
contextNote: Authored schematic course represents the common intracranial path, not each inner-ear branch or a validated labyrinth. Sensory nerve central projections and reflex efferents are distinguished.

name: CN IX Glossopharyngeal nerve
modality: Branchial motor, preganglionic parasympathetic, taste, visceral afferent and general sensory.
course: Rootlets emerge from the postolivary sulcus of the medulla and exit the skull through the jugular foramen. Superior/inferior sensory ganglia lie near this exit. Branches reach the stylopharyngeus, pharynx/posterior tongue, carotid sinus/body and tympanic-otic parasympathetic route.
function: Supplies stylopharyngeus; conveys posterior-third tongue taste and pharyngeal general sensation; carries carotid sinus/body sensory input. Inferior salivatory axons reach the otic ganglion via tympanic and lesser petrosal routes, then the parotid through auriculotemporal nerve. CN IX commonly supplies a gag-reflex afferent limb, with vagal motor output.

afferent: Superior/inferior sensory ganglion afferents: taste/visceral signals to solitary nucleus and general sensory signals to spinal trigeminal complex
efferent: Nucleus ambiguus motor fibers to stylopharyngeus
Inferior salivatory preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to otic ganglion and then parotid gland

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Posterior tongue/pharyngeal sensory or taste loss and impaired gag afference may occur. Gag responses vary normally and their absence alone does not establish a IX lesion. Combined IX/X lesions can impair swallowing.

Brief severe pain in throat, posterior tongue or ear may be triggered by swallowing or talking. Occasionally vagal cardioinhibitory reflexes accompany attacks; this is not the expected consequence of simply losing IX sensory input.
Mass, inflammation or vascular injury near the jugular foramen may combine IX/X/XI deficits. The pattern suggests a region but does not establish one cause.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
contextNote: Authored schematic root/jugular course. The principal parasympathetic source is inferior salivatory nucleus; DMV is a vagal nucleus and is not substituted as IX secretomotor origin.

name: CN X Vagus nerve
modality: Branchial motor, preganglionic parasympathetic, visceral afferent, taste and small general sensory components.
course: Postolivary medullary rootlets leave through the jugular foramen with superior/inferior sensory ganglia. The vagus descends in the carotid sheath and gives pharyngeal, superior laryngeal, recurrent laryngeal, cardiac and thoracoabdominal branches. Right recurrent laryngeal loops under right subclavian artery; left loops under the aortic arch.
function: Motor supply to palate except tensor veli palatini, pharynx except stylopharyngeus, and larynx; external superior laryngeal supplies cricothyroid while recurrent laryngeal supplies other intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Visceral afferents reach solitary nucleus and parasympathetic axons regulate thoracoabdominal organs. Cardiac vagal neurons include an important ambiguus source; DMV contributes particularly to abdominal visceral control. The auricular sensory branch is Arnold nerve.

afferent: Superior/inferior vagal sensory ganglia: visceral/taste inputs to solitary nucleus and general sensory input to spinal trigeminal complex
efferent: Ambiguus branchiomotor neurons to palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles
Preganglionic cardiac vagal neurons including ambiguus region
DMV and other vagal parasympathetic outflow to ganglia near thoracoabdominal viscera

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Unilateral palatal and vocal-fold weakness can cause hoarseness, dysphagia and aspiration; the palate may sag ipsilaterally and uvula deviate away from the weak side. Severity and gag responses vary.

Recurrent laryngeal injury can impair vocal-fold movement. External superior laryngeal/cricothyroid injury particularly impairs pitch modulation. Surgery or lesions along neck/chest courses can affect these branches.

Vagal network injury can disturb cardiovascular and gastrointestinal regulation. Bradycardia from increased vagal activity is not equivalent to loss of parasympathetic neurons, which should not be presented as causing inevitable bradycardia/asystole.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
contextNote: Authored schematic common nerve; recurrent laryngeal and abdominal branches are not individually reconstructed. The classic cranial-XI root is functionally vagal, separate from spinal XI shoulder fibers.

name: CN XI Accessory nerve
modality: Motor to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (spinal accessory component).
course: Spinal accessory rootlets arise from upper cervical spinal cord segments, approximately C1-C5/6. They ascend through the foramen magnum and leave through the jugular foramen, then supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Medullary rootlets historically termed cranial XI are functionally part of the vagus.
function: Supports head turning through sternocleidomastoid and shoulder elevation/scapular movement through trapezius. The spinal nerve is distinct from vagal branchiomotor supply to palate/pharynx/larynx.

afferent: Spinal accessory motor nucleus in upper cervical cord, with descending motor control
efferent: Ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; cervical plexus contributes additional fibers/proprioception

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Trapezius weakness can cause shoulder droop, impaired shrug and scapular dysfunction; sternocleidomastoid weakness impairs turning the head away from the weak muscle side. Deficits depend on lesion position. Posterior-triangle surgery/trauma is a recognized cause.
Combined IX/X/XI deficits suggest a skull-base region; isolated trapezius weakness can occur farther along the spinal accessory course. No single vascular cause is implied by the pattern.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
contextNote: Authored schematic course; a medullary surface waypoint does not represent the true spinal motor origin. Upper cervical rootlets and foramen-magnum entry require separate geometry to be anatomically faithful.

name: CN XII Hypoglossal nerve
course: Motor neurons in the hypoglossal nucleus send fascicles ventrally through the medulla, emerging in the preolivary sulcus between pyramid and olive. The nerve exits through the hypoglossal canal and courses toward the tongue. C1 spinal fibers briefly join its extracranial course.
function: Supplies intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus (vagus). C1 fibers traveling with XII reach geniohyoid and thyrohyoid and contribute to ansa cervicalis; these are spinal fibers, not axons arising from the hypoglossal nucleus.

afferent: Hypoglossal somatic motor neurons; corticobulbar/reticular control terminates centrally.
efferent: C1 accompanying fibers to geniohyoid/thyrohyoid and ansa cervicalis, distinguished from true XII fibers

bloodSupply: Small segmental vessels along the intracranial, skull-base and extracranial course supply the nerve. Adjacent large arteries and the vascular supply of the brainstem nucleus are not synonymous with the peripheral nerve territory; a precise segment-by-segment map is not represented here.

clinical.findings: Nuclear, fascicular or nerve injury can weaken the ipsilateral tongue, which tends to deviate toward the weak side on protrusion. Atrophy and fasciculations may develop with lower motor neuron disease or chronic denervation.

A unilateral supranuclear lesion often weakens the contralateral tongue, with protrusion toward the weak side. Medial medullary lesions can combine ipsilateral XII weakness and contralateral limb weakness/sensory deficits. Neck/skull-base causes require localization along the nerve rather than one assumed artery.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
contextNote: Authored schematic course from medullary exit to canal/tongue; no specimen-segmented canal or tongue reconstruction. Tongue deviation laterality depends on lower versus upper motor neuron injury.
